title: Warmup latency heatmap + bucketization labbook
content:
Purpose:
Quick personal log for a set of microbench runs exploring warmup dynamics when we bucket incoming requests by token-length and session-history depth. Trying to capture visual-ish heatmaps (ASCII), runtime config, and immediate hypotheses for follow-ups. Intended as a labbook — messy, partial, and reproducible-ish.

Background / Why this felt useful:
- We see a recurring pattern: short requests (<= 32 tokens) get aggressively batched and warm quickly; mid-length (33–128) show much more sensitive p95 behavior depending on cache priming; long (>128) dominate GPU memory and cause evictions that ripple into subsequent short requests.
- Suspect that naive bucketing (single token-length buckets) is suboptimal when session-history (KV cache size) varies. Idea: two-dimensional bucketization (token_length x kv_entries) and observe warmup time and steady-state p95.

Experiment configuration (single-node dev rig):
- Model: open-llama-7B-ish (quantized q4_0 build)
- GPU: A100-40GB (dev pool instance)
- Runtime: runtime branch heatmap-warmup-v3 (see PR above)
- Load generator: locust-style harness, Poisson arrivals, adjustable session seeds
- Duration: 18 runs * 10 minutes each (5m ramp, 5m steady capture)
- Buckets:
  - token_length buckets: [0-32, 33-64, 65-128, 129-512]
  - kv_entries buckets: [0, 1-4, 5-16, 17+]
- Mix: each run focuses on one token_length bucket but randomizes kv_entries according to target distribution for that run
- Metric capture: p50, p90, p95, p99, cold-call-rate,KV-hit-rate, GPU mem high-water

Run notes (timestamps relative to run start):
- Warmup stage (first ~60–90s): continuous drop in p95 for short-token buckets when kv_entries=0. If kv_entries>8 the p95 initially spikes and takes ~3x longer to stabilize.
- Eviction event observed on run 7 at t=4:12 caused by two concurrent long requests -> immediate p99 spike across all buckets for ~30s. Correlated with mem HWM jump to 98%.
- Some runs showed a non-monotonic warmup: small oscillations in p90 caused by mixing policy that forced cross-bucket coalescing (we use a soft-threshold to allow batching across neighbouring buckets).

Representative ASCII heatmaps (rows = kv_entries buckets 0..3, cols = token length buckets 0..3). Cell = p95 at 5m steady-state (ms).
[Legend: rows 0..3 => 0,1-4,5-16,17+; cols 0..3 => <=32,33-64,65-128,129-512]

Heatmap run A (baseline batch-size 16, no cross-coalesce):
  48   62   110  420
  55   75   150  530
  90   140  310  980
  120  210  700  1800

Heatmap run B (soft cross-coalesce enabled, threshold 0.25):
  42   58   98   380
  48   70   130  470
  82   125  280  860
  110  190  640  1600

Immediate takeaways from heatmaps:
- Cross-coalescing helps especially in low-kv/short-token cells; p95 improves ~10–12% there.
- High-kv & long-token cells still dominate tail latency; when they trigger evictions, the whole table shifts up for ~30–90s (depending on mem pressure).
- There's a smooth gradient across token-length and kv depth — good sign that a small number of bucket shapes can capture most variance.

Observations (quick bullets):
- Cold-call-rate for short-token/no-kv bucket was ~3% in run A, ~1.2% in run B.
- KV-hit-rate correlates strongly with p95 improvements — suggests we should prioritize cache priming for mid-length sessions to lower rolling p95.
- Eviction recovery time scales superlinearly with the size of objects evicted (duh), but also depends on incoming request mix during recovery window — a steady trickle of long requests prevents quick recovery.

Sketch of next experiments (ordered):
1) Controlled eviction test: deliberately trigger eviction via long synthetic requests then flood with short-token requests and measure recovery curves under different prefetch strategies.
2) Adaptive bucket migration: when a bucket's p95 stays >X for Y seconds, split it or shift boundaries; test convergence and stability.
3) Cold-prime policy: for known high-traffic sessions, pre-warm KV cache on idle capacity (simulate with background priming agents).
4) Cost vs latency: repeat runs under quantized 8-bit runtime vs q4_0 to measure tradeoffs in p95 and memory churn.

Quick TODOs (me / collaborators):
- [ ] Push small reproducer script into bench repo (PR draft in linked_artifacts) — I started it in the branch but need to clean up flags.
- [ ] Add a Prometheus dashboard tile that renders p95 heatmap by token-length x kv-depth (query sketch in the branch notes).
- [ ] File an SRE playbook snippet for eviction recovery thresholds (auto-notify when mem HWM > 92% and p99 > 1.2s).
- [ ] Longer: build an RL-ish policy that nudges bucket boundaries to minimize expected p95 under current mix (research spike).

Open questions / hypotheses to validate:
- Is the additional complexity of kv-aware buckets worth the operational cost vs a simple TTL-based prefetch? Metric to compare: steady-state p95 improvement per 1% increase in operational surface area (heuristic).
- How often do we see mixed-request arrivals in prod that would actually benefit from cross-coalesce? Production ingress traces needed (ask telemetry team for 7-day sample).

Notes to self:
- When exporting heatmaps for Slack/Confluence, create a small color legend (reds are >500ms). The ASCII is useful for quick iteration but not great for stakeholder communication.
- Keep this file lightweight; formalize into a Confluence page if the eviction-recovery test shows >20% improvement from priming.

Appendix: raw numbers snapshot (run B steady-state p95 table ms):
- (0,<=32) = 42ms; (0,33-64)=58ms; (0,65-128)=98ms; (0,129-512)=380ms
- (1,<=32) = 48ms; (1,33-64)=70ms; (1,65-128)=130ms; (1,129-512)=470ms
- (2,<=32) = 82ms; (2,33-64)=125ms; (2,65-128)=280ms; (2,129-512)=860ms
- (3,<=32) = 110ms; (3,33-64)=190ms; (3,65-128)=640ms; (3,129-512)=1600ms
